name: Grace Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the water cart most days at a big bauxite mine, and on a haul truck when they need me. The water cart sprays the haul roads so the dust stays down, which sounds simple, but too much water and the trucks slide, too little and you can't see your hand. I start at half six, fill up at the standpipe, and do my loops all day, radioing the pit controller. I like being trusted with it and I like the early mornings when the red dirt looks almost purple, and what wears me out is the heat in the cab when the air conditioning plays up.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Murat has a little plumbing business, just him and an apprentice, and I do his invoices on Sunday nights. We've got Ayla, fourteen, and Kerem, ten. Saturdays I'm at the junior football club running the canteen, it's where half the town catches up. My daughter put an AI app on my phone last year and I use it now and then, mostly to tidy up Murat's quotes so they don't sound like he wrote them on a ute bonnet, which he does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because a lot of people were getting carried away. I'd say the company's better off spending money on fixing the air conditioning than on fancy computers. At the canteen I'd say it with a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd be happy to keep doing my loops until the kids are through school. I'm not someone who needs a big change to feel alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Keep my savings ticking, we've got about four months, and keep doing Murat's books. Maybe use the AI app a bit more for his invoices, since it saves me an hour on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the app more for Murat's invoices. Does he know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He does now. He was suspicious at first, he said, who's reading our business. I told him it's only writing the nice words, the numbers are still mine. He's a traditional man, like me, but he likes his Sunday nights back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that there's already talk of driverless water carts at a couple of other mines. That's not AI hype, that's just the machines getting better. I'd keep an eye on it, but I'm not losing sleep.

S0.say: I'd say it's good, because people were getting carried away. The company should spend money on air conditioning, not fancy computers.
S0.think: It's fine for me and I'd be happy to keep doing my water cart loops until the kids finish school. I don't need big change.
S0.do: Keeps working, keeps about four months of savings ticking along and keeps doing her husband's books. Uses the AI app more for his invoices to save an hour on Sundays.
S0.quote: The company's better off spending money on fixing the air conditioning than on fancy computers.
S0.fieldNote: Grace is content and practical, and she already uses AI in a small, tested way for the family business. She tells AI hype apart from real machine changes she's heard of. Her husband's business is an important second leg for the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has a duty to look after the people who've worked hard for it. Train us up, don't just push us out. I'd say it to the supervisor and at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think water carts are an easy one to automate, it's a loop on a road. I'd probably have a few years. But I'm not one to sit and worry, I'd want to know what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about any training for the new driverless systems once a few others had done it and said it was useful. I'd talk to Murat about me doing more in the business, maybe the bookings and some of the simple jobs. And we'd put an extra hundred a fortnight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but practical uneasy. I'd make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do more in Murat's business. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bookings, quotes, chasing payments, which he hates. Maybe even learn some of the basic work, tap washers and that. He's been saying for years he needs someone to answer the phone, so it might be a blessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kevin on the other water cart, he's fifty-eight and widowed and the job's his whole week. He's not a reader, and he doesn't have a family business to fall back on. I'd want the company to look after him, and if they didn't, the club would have to.

S1.say: I'd say the company has a duty to look after people who've worked hard for it. They should train us up, not push us out.
S1.think: Water carts are easy to automate because they just loop a road, so I'd have a few years. I'm not one to sit and worry, I'd want to know what's next.
S1.do: Takes training on driverless systems once others say it's useful and plans a bigger role in her husband's plumbing business. Adds about a hundred a fortnight to savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy in a practical way, making a list.
S1.quote: He's been saying for years he needs someone to answer the phone, so it might be a blessing.
S1.fieldNote: Grace's traditional outlook shows in expecting the company and community, not government, to look after people. She'd move once change is proven and already has a family business to move toward. She worries for a widowed older colleague without that backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is far too fast and someone should have put the brakes on. I'd say families need to stick together through it. I wouldn't be asking for handouts, I'd be asking for time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job's gone and Murat's too, eventually, if robots can do plumbing. That's both our incomes. Two years isn't enough to work out a new life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every extra we've got, the club fees, the takeaway Friday, the new fridge. I'd work full time in Murat's business while plumbers are still needed, getting him as many jobs as we can. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move in with them if the mortgage got too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at two in the morning doing the sums on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the two-year warning change things, compared with ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten I'd do a proper trade course and Murat could slowly change the business. With two, we'd just be scrambling. It's like trying to change a tyre while you're still driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't ask for handouts. What if there was government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if I had to, for the kids. But I'd feel ashamed, and I'd want it to be short. My father worked two jobs to keep us off the dole, and I'd hear his voice every time.

S2.say: I'd say this is far too fast and someone should have put on the brakes. Families need to stick together, and I'd ask for time, not handouts.
S2.think: My job is gone, and my husband's plumbing work eventually too if robots can do it. That's both incomes, and two years isn't enough for a new life.
S2.do: Cuts club fees, takeaway nights and a new fridge, and works full time in her husband's business while plumbers are still needed. Asks her parents about moving in if the mortgage gets too much.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at two in the morning doing sums at the kitchen table.
S2.quote: It's like trying to change a tyre while you're still driving.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture threatens both household incomes, which is what pushes Grace to alarm. She'd lean on family first and accept government help only with shame, echoing her father. She stays organised even in fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's get the young ones into apprenticeships now, while there's still time. I'd say families should be planning together. I'd say it at the club and to anyone at the mine who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives us time for one change. I'd stay on the water cart while it lasts and learn plumbing properly, so the business could carry two of us. Whether plumbing lasts past 2031, I don't know, but it would last longer than the water cart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into a mature-age plumbing apprenticeship with Murat as my supervisor, starting next year once I'd talked to a couple of women who've done it. I'd keep the savings growing toward six months. And we'd pay off the ute so the business has no debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Like before a big exam you've studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A mature-age apprenticeship is a big step. What would make you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talking to people who've done it. There's a woman at church, Lena, who did electrical at forty. If she says it's doable with kids, I'd believe her. I'm not going to jump just because a website says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ayla and Kerem think of their mum becoming a plumber?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ayla would be embarrassed for about a week and then she'd tell everyone. Kerem would want to come on jobs. I'd like them to see their mum learn something new at forty-five, that's a good lesson.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to get the young ones into apprenticeships now. Families should be planning together.
S3.think: Five years is time for one change. I'd stay on the water cart while it lasts and learn plumbing properly, which would last longer even if I don't know for how long.
S3.do: Starts a mature-age plumbing apprenticeship next year with her husband supervising, after talking to people who've done it. Grows savings toward six months and pays off the business ute.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, like before an exam she's studied for.
S3.quote: I'd like them to see their mum learn something new at forty-five, that's a good lesson.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Grace commits to a real change but still checks it with someone she trusts first, which is typical of her steady style. The family business gives her a concrete path. She sees her own retraining as a lesson for her kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do things properly, so no excuses. Bring back apprenticeships, keep families strong, and the companies should help pay. I'd say that at the club and in the voting booth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three. I could do the plumbing apprenticeship at a normal pace and work alongside Murat for years. It's not the end of the world for us, more a long change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the water cart for a few years while I study plumbing part time. Murat and I would plan to grow the business, maybe take on a second apprentice. And we'd talk to Ayla about her future, she wants to be a vet nurse and I'd back that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Like knowing winter's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to rush and get it wrong. I'd have time to see how the robots are going and whether plumbing's really safe. If it isn't, I'd still have time to try something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd back Ayla being a vet nurse. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people will always want a person holding their dog when it's sick. And she's gentle with animals, always has been. I'd rather she did something she loves than something someone says is safe.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do things properly, with apprenticeships back and strong families. Companies should help pay, and I'd say so at the club and the ballot box.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three and could do the plumbing apprenticeship at a normal pace and work alongside my husband for years. It's not the end of the world, more a long change.
S4.do: Keeps driving the water cart for a few years while studying plumbing part time. Plans to grow the family business with a second apprentice and backs her daughter's plan to be a vet nurse.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, like knowing winter is coming.
S4.quote: Because people will always want a person holding their dog when it's sick.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Grace's plan into a gradual shift into the family business. She thinks the time mostly buys her the chance to avoid mistakes. She values her daughter's love of animals over chasing a safe job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both Murat and I would be in trouble at once. What would help is apprenticeships that adults can actually do while working, and companies helping families through it rather than leaving it all to the government. And honest timelines, so we can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the women out here. There's more of us on the water carts and trucks than people think. We're the ones who'd be juggling the kids and the change at the same time.

headlineQuote: We're the ones who'd be juggling the kids and the change at the same time.
portrait: Grace Yilmaz is a 43-year-old water cart and haul truck operator at a large bauxite mine, married to Murat, who runs a small plumbing business she helps run on Sunday nights. She's traditional and family-centred, expects the company and community to look after people, and would only accept government help with shame. She stays calm or uneasy in the milder pictures and is alarmed in the two-year one, where both household incomes are at risk. With more time she'd do a mature-age plumbing apprenticeship, after checking with people she trusts, and fold herself into the family business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both her income and her husband's would be at risk at once.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships adults can do while working, companies helping families through the change, and honest timelines to plan by.
